subChunks.title: PgBouncer and Connection Management
subChunks.hookHtml: Each PostgreSQL connection consumes ~5–10MB of RAM and spawns a process. At 1,000 concurrent connections, PostgreSQL spends more time managing connections than running queries. A connection pooler solves this.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why connections are expensive

PostgreSQL uses a process-per-connection model. Each connection: forks a backend process, allocates memory for the process context, and maintains a slot in pg_stat_activity. At high concurrency, context switching between hundreds of processes degrades throughput.

PgBouncer — the standard pooler

PgBouncer sits between application and PostgreSQL, maintaining a small pool of actual database connections. Many application connections share a few real database connections.

Pooling modes

  • Session pooling — one server connection per client session. Same as no pooling. Used for legacy compatibility.
  • Transaction pooling — server connection assigned for the duration of a transaction only. One server connection can serve many clients between transactions. Most common production mode.
  • Statement pooling — server connection released after each statement. Requires all queries to be auto-committed. Rarely used.
; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
arcane = host=db.internal port=5432 dbname=arcane

[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 1000
default_pool_size = 20  -- 20 real connections to PostgreSQL

Transaction pooling caveats

With transaction pooling, session-level features do not persist between transactions: prepared statements, SET LOCAL, advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and temporary tables. Design your application to be stateless within each transaction.

Neon and serverless pooling

Serverless databases like Neon have built-in connection poolers. Neon scales connections automatically and can handle thousands of short-lived serverless function connections without overwhelming PostgreSQL.

storyBeats.text: The application has 500 serverless functions each opening a connection. PostgreSQL shows 500 idle connections consuming 3GB RAM.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: PostgreSQL was never designed for thousands of direct connections. PgBouncer is the membrane between your application's connection hunger and PostgreSQL's connection reality. Twenty real connections serving a thousand application connections — each only borrowing one for the duration of their transaction.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Connection pool sizing

An API server handles 500 req/s, each request uses one database transaction averaging 5ms. Calculate: (1) the theoretical minimum server connections needed, (2) why you would set default_pool_size higher, (3) what happens when all pool connections are occupied.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Theoretical minimum (Little's Law):
Connections needed = arrival rate × average hold time
= 500 req/s × 0.005s = 2.5 connections
With overhead: ~5 connections theoretically sufficient.

(2) Why set higher (e.g. 20):
- Traffic is bursty — 500 req/s average but 2000 req/s peaks
- Some requests take longer (slow queries, complex transactions)
- Connection establishment overhead during burst
- Buffer for variance: p99 response time may be 50ms, requiring 500 × 0.050 = 25 connections at peak
Typical rule: set pool_size = (CPU cores × 2) + disk count, or benchmark empirically. For PostgreSQL on a 4-core server, 10-20 is a reasonable starting point.

(3) When all connections are occupied:
PgBouncer queues new requests (up to the wait queue limit). Clients wait until a connection is available. If the queue fills or wait timeout is exceeded, new connections are refused with an error. Monitor: pgbouncer's pool_size utilisation should stay below 80% at peak.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain why prepared statements and LISTEN/NOTIFY do not work reliably with PgBouncer transaction-mode pooling, and describe the workaround for each.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Prepared statements: In session mode, a prepared statement is created once per session and reused. In transaction mode, after a transaction commits, the server connection returns to the pool and may be given to a different client. The next client using that connection has no prepared statement. Workaround: use protocol-level prepared statements via the client library (they are re-prepared per server connection by drivers like pgx) or disable server-side prepared statements.

LISTEN/NOTIFY: LISTEN registers a subscription on a specific server connection. In transaction mode, the server connection is recycled between transactions. The LISTEN subscription disappears when the connection returns to the pool. Workaround: use a dedicated long-lived connection outside PgBouncer for LISTEN subscriptions, or use a separate session-mode pool for notification consumers.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a connection pooler does, why it is needed for PostgreSQL in high-concurrency environments, and the trade-offs between session and transaction pooling modes.

options: A server connection is assigned to a client only for the duration of a transaction — released back to the pool after COMMIT or ROLLBACK
Each client has a dedicated server connection for their entire session
One server connection is shared by all clients simultaneously
Connections are pooled per database table
questions.answer: A server connection is assigned to a client only for the duration of a transaction — released back to the pool after COMMIT or ROLLBACK
questions.explanation: Transaction-mode pooling is the most efficient mode: the expensive server connection is borrowed only for the duration of active work. Between transactions, the client is not holding a server connection.

questions.prompt: Using Little's Law: 200 req/s, each holding a connection for 10ms. How many server connections are needed?
questions.explanation: Little's Law: L = λ × W. Connections = 200 req/s × 0.010s = 2. In practice you add margin for variance and bursts, but the theoretical minimum is 2. This shows that most connections are idle most of the time — pooling multiplexes them efficiently.

questions.prompt: A developer uses `SET LOCAL search_path = myschema` inside a transaction with PgBouncer in transaction mode. Why is this unreliable?
options: SET LOCAL only applies for the current transaction — when the connection returns to the pool, the next client may have a different search_path expectation
SET LOCAL is not supported inside transactions
PgBouncer does not forward SET commands
questions.answer: SET LOCAL only applies for the current transaction — when the connection returns to the pool, the next client may have a different search_path expectation
questions.explanation: SET LOCAL correctly expires at transaction end. The problem is the reverse: if another part of your code sets search_path at SESSION level (SET search_path), that change persists on the server connection even after the transaction ends. The next client picks up a polluted connection. Transaction-mode pooling requires stateless server connections — no session-level settings that persist.

questions.prompt: A serverless function opens a new database connection for each invocation. 1000 functions run concurrently. What is the right architecture?
options: A connection pooler (PgBouncer or built-in like Neon's pooler) in front of PostgreSQL — functions connect to the pooler, which maintains a fixed pool of actual DB connections
Each function should use a persistent process with a connection pool
Use SQLite instead of PostgreSQL for serverless
questions.answer: A connection pooler (PgBouncer or built-in like Neon's pooler) in front of PostgreSQL — functions connect to the pooler, which maintains a fixed pool of actual DB connections
questions.explanation: Serverless functions cannot maintain persistent connections. Each invocation starts fresh. A connection pooler accepts all 1000 connections but multiplexes them through 20 actual PostgreSQL connections. Increasing max_connections to 1000 in PostgreSQL allocates 5–10MB RAM per connection = 5–10GB RAM just for idle connections.
